# Qwen3-8B (LLM, Qwen3ForCausalLM) - MI300X Standalone Analysis

## Executive Summary

This is a single-trace roofline analysis of a vLLM prefill/decode steady-state window for Qwen3-8B on MI300X, covering 1718.37 ms of GPU timeline across four forward passes (token batches 8192, 8192, 7209 and 1072). The GPU is busy for only 49.15% of the window; the remaining 50.85% is idle, and that idle is host-side — exposed collective communication is 0.00% and exposed device transfer is 0.006%, so neither collectives nor copies explain it. Of the 844.55 ms of compute, GEMM dominates at 630.23 ms (74.6% of compute time), followed by paged attention at 121.36 ms (14.4%) and RMSNorm at 48.51 ms (5.7%). The BF16 projection GEMMs are already healthy at 60-82% of the 708 TFLOPS matrix-BF16 roofline, so the largest kernel-level headroom sits in the paged-attention prefill kernel (9-10% of roofline) and the narrow-row RMSNorm kernels (12-17% of the 5.3 TB/s HBM roofline). The single biggest opportunity in the trace is not a kernel at all: 691.5 ms of host dispatch time in excess of kernel time accounts for 79.1% of the idle window.

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Total Time | 1718.37 ms |
| Compute % | 49.15% |
| Idle % | 50.85% |
| Exposed Communication % | 0.00% |
| Top Bottleneck Category | GEMM (74.6%) |

![Performance Improvement](data:image/png;base64,)

---
## Compute Kernel Optimizations

Findings from per-category kernel analysis (GEMM, paged attention, RMSNorm, elementwise, Triton, reduce, other).
Summaries of recommendations from the Step 8 sub-agents, focused on individual kernel efficiency.

### Top Operations

| Rank | Category | Time (ms) | % of Compute Time | Ops |
|------|----------|-----------|-------------------|-----|
| 1 | GEMM | 630.229 | 74.62% | 14 | <!-- top-ops-row low=6.06 high=8.07 -->
| 2 | InferenceAttention | 121.357 | 14.37% | 3 | <!-- top-ops-row low=4.48 high=5.97 -->
| 3 | RMSNorm | 48.507 | 5.74% | 12 | <!-- top-ops-row low=1.08 high=1.43 -->
<!-- impact-end -->

### 🔴 P1: Compute-bound BF16 projections leaving roofline headroom (Tensile)

**Insight**: Ten compute-bound BF16 GEMM signatures in the Qwen3 decoder projections run at 60-82% of the 708 TFLOPS matrix-BF16 roofline, leaving 606.2 ms of kernel time with measurable headroom.

**Action**: Profile the dominant member kernels for tile-size and wave-occupancy tuning, starting with the 8192x24576x4096 gate/up projection that consumes 214.72 ms on its own. If the model tolerates a narrower precision than BF16, moving these projections to FP8 would lower the compute floor, since the platform's FP8 matrix peak is 1273 TFLOPS against 708 TFLOPS for BF16.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item category=gemm low=6.06 mid=7.07 high=8.07 -->
**Impact**: impact_score: 7.07
<!-- impact-end -->

→ *See [Detailed Analysis: Compute kernel insights > P1](#detailed-analysis-compute-p1) for details*

---

### 🟡 P2: Long-sequence paged attention prefill kernel far below compute roofline

**Insight**: The 8192-token paged-attention operation consumes 81.484 ms of GPU kernel time at 9.01% of the bf16 matrix roofline, and its `_fwd_kernel` prefill component accounts for 91.85% of that time.

**Action**: Profile the `_fwd_kernel` prefill component for tile-size tuning at the 8192-token shape. Enable chunked prefill so that per-step prefill work is bounded, and confirm the kernel groups the 4:1 GQA query heads efficiently rather than replaying KV reads per query head.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item category=inferenceattention low=3.24 mid=3.78 high=4.31 -->
**Impact**: impact_score: 3.78
<!-- impact-end -->

→ *See [Detailed Analysis: Compute kernel insights > P2](#detailed-analysis-compute-p2) for details*

---

### 🟢 P3: Mid-length paged attention operation far below memory roofline

**Insight**: The 7209-token paged-attention operation spends 31.756 ms of GPU kernel time at 10.42% of the HBM bandwidth roofline, with `_fwd_kernel` again dominating at 87.72% of operation time.

**Action**: Optimize the memory access pattern of the `_fwd_kernel` prefill component at this shape, and batch the 7209-token and 8192-token requests onto a common tuned configuration so a single tile schedule serves both. Increasing the decode batch size amortizes KV-cache reads across more queries per pass.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item category=inferenceattention low=1.24 mid=1.45 high=1.66 -->
**Impact**: impact_score: 1.45
<!-- impact-end -->

→ *See [Detailed Analysis: Compute kernel insights > P3](#detailed-analysis-compute-p3) for details*

---

### 🟢 P4: Narrow-row RMSNorm running far below the bandwidth roofline (AITER)

**Insight**: Six `aiter::rms_norm` signatures that normalize 128-element rows deliver only 11.7-17.0% of the 5.3 TB/s HBM roofline, costing 28.0 ms of GPU kernel time.

**Action**: Optimize the memory access pattern of the dominant `aiter::add_rmsnorm_quant_kernel` instantiation (the 64-wide template variant) so each launch streams more contiguous bytes per row group. For chains of memory-bound operations inside the same parent module (norm plus activation plus residual), defer to the kernel fusion analysis rather than tuning them in isolation.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item category=rmsnorm low=1.08 mid=1.25 high=1.43 -->
**Impact**: impact_score: 1.25
<!-- impact-end -->

→ *See [Detailed Analysis: Compute kernel insights > P4](#detailed-analysis-compute-p4) for details*

---
## Kernel Fusion Opportunities (Experimental)

> **Note:** Kernel fusion analysis is experimental. impact_score projections estimate the recoverable fraction of E2E with 85% memory/compute pipeline overlap. Kernels without perf models use their measured trace time as-is. Candidates where fewer than 75% of kernels have perf models are not reported. Actual recoverable time depends on implementation feasibility and interaction effects.

No kernel fusion opportunities detected.

The deterministic fusion scan surfaced 14 raw candidates and narrowed them to 2, neither of which cleared the minimum impact gate against the 1718.37 ms baseline. The largest surviving candidate is a whole decoder-layer container (12 kernels, 690.4 ms) whose normalization work is already folded into `aiter::add_rmsnorm_quant_kernel` and whose activation work is already folded into `triton_poi_fused_mul_silu_slice_0`. The second candidate, the RMSNorm implementation path (2 kernels, 34.5 ms over 288 instances), is bounded above by roughly 2.0% of E2E even at 100% savings and falls below the gate once the roofline gap is applied. This workload's norm and activation paths are already running fused AITER and Triton kernels.

---
## System-Level Optimizations

> **Note:** System-level analysis is exploratory. The patterns and recommendations below are under active development and may be refined as system-level analysis matures.

Findings from system-level analysis (GPU utilization, memory transfer patterns,
communication/compute overlap). These affect the GPU pipeline as a whole.

Multi-kernel analysis returned no actionable issue: memory-copy time is 0.11 ms (0.01% of the timeline) across 32 events, there are zero device-to-host transfers, and the trace contains no collective communication events at all, so all three multi-kernel assessments are unflagged. The 50.85% idle time that dominates this timeline is a host-pipeline concern and is captured in the two priorities below rather than double-counted as a data-movement issue.

### 🔴 P1: Replay the forward pass from a captured GPU graph

**Insight**: The host spends 691.5 ms more inside operation dispatch than the GPU spends running the kernels those dispatches launch, and that excess accounts for 79.1% of the 873.7 ms idle window.

**Action**: Enable full-graph capture for the model forward path so one host submission replays an entire pass, and pad incoming batches to the captured shape buckets. Where capture is not possible for the largest mixed batches, cut the number of dispatches per layer instead by merging the normalization, cache-write and activation chain into fewer submissions.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item low=null mid=null high=null -->
**Impact**: Not quantifiable from trace data
<!-- impact-end -->

→ *See [Detailed Analysis: System-level insights > P1](#detailed-analysis-system-p1) for details*

---

### 🟡 P2: Move host-side preparation out of the per-layer attention wrapper

**Insight**: The attention wrapper holds the host for 1.23 ms longer per call than its own kernels run, which is the largest per-invocation host gap in the trace.

**Action**: Hoist the attention metadata preparation and shape-dependent branching out of the per-layer call and compute it once per forward pass, so the per-layer call reduces to a kernel submission.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item low=null mid=null high=null -->
**Impact**: Not quantifiable from trace data

### Compute Kernel Insights

All ten come from the same operation and the same launcher inside the model's linear-layer utility path, and all dispatch to the Tensile backend. The module chain places every one of them in the Qwen3 causal language model decoder stack: the weight shapes identify the fused gate/up projection (24576x4096), the down projection (4096x12288), the fused QKV projection (6144x4096), and the attention output projection (4096x4096). None of them reaches the 708 TFLOPS matrix-BF16 roofline. The best member achieves 82.48% of that peak on the 8192x4096x12288 down projection, and the weakest reaches only 60.08% on the 1072x6144x4096 decode-shape QKV projection. Efficiency falls monotonically as the token count drops: the three decode-sized signatures at M = 1072 sit between 60% and 67%, whereas the prefill-sized signatures at M = 7209 and M = 8192 sit between 72% and 82%. That pattern is consistent with the smaller M dimension producing fewer output tiles and thus less work to spread across the device. The single largest cost is the 8192x24576x4096 fused gate/up projection at 214.72 ms over 72 invocations, which is 12.5% of end-to-end GPU time on its own. Tile size is not visible in the trace beyond the kernel-name encoding, so the selected tiling cannot be validated here. Decomposition strategy is not visible — profile the kernel for tiling layout.

**Resolution:** Tile-size and wave-occupancy tuning helps because the roofline gap on these kernels is a scheduling problem rather than a data-movement problem. At 746 to 2458 FLOPS/Byte the kernels already move very few bytes per FLOP, so the missing throughput comes from matrix cores that are idle during part of the kernel. A tile shape that divides the output matrix into a tile count closer to a whole multiple of the device's compute units reduces the tail wave in which most units have no tile left to process. This matters most for the low-M decode shapes, where the total tile count is smallest and a partial final wave costs proportionally more. Narrowing precision from BF16 to FP8 attacks the problem from the other side: the matrix-core peak rises from 708 to 1273 TFLOPS, so the same FLOP count has a lower floor on execution time, and the weight bytes fetched per invocation halve. Kernel running slower than expected — profile occupancy with hardware counters. Bottleneck identified — generate reproducer for kernel team.

This sequence length sits well above the 4096-token band where a tuned attention kernel would be expected to reach a substantially higher fraction of roofline. Flash tile size not visible — profile the kernel for tile-size tuning. Large working set may exceed cache. Per-request KV-cache hit rate not visible from trace data.

**Resolution:** Improving the access pattern of the prefill kernel raises the fraction of each fetched cache line that is actually consumed, so the same attention math completes with fewer bytes pulled from HBM. Routing the 7209-token and 8192-token shapes to a common tuned configuration is worthwhile because both are dominated by the same `_fwd_kernel` at a near-identical head geometry, so one tuning pass amortizes over 113 ms of kernel time instead of 32 ms. Raising the decode batch size lets a single pass over a KV-cache block serve more queries, which spreads a fixed KV read cost across more useful output tokens. Tuning the KV-cache block size is not indicated here because the `reshape_and_cache` component does not appear in this operation's kernel breakdown.

Each of these signatures normalizes rows of 128 elements, which matches the per-head normalization applied to query and key projections rather than the model-width normalization applied to the residual stream. Reduction strategy is not visible from the trace, so profile the kernel to identify the variant. Root causes generally are not visible in a trace, which shows what is slow rather than why.

### System-Level Insights

<a id="detailed-analysis-system-p1"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=system rank=1 -->
#### 🔴 P1: Per-dispatch host overhead paces the forward pass instead of the GPU

**Identification:** The idle share of the profiled window exceeded the 15% flag threshold, so the window was examined for the source of the gap. Exposed communication and exposed device-transfer time are both effectively zero, which rules out collectives and host-device copies as the cause. Summing host-side operation duration against kernel time across all seven compute categories shows the host holding each operation far longer than its kernels run, and six of the seven categories were independently flagged for this. The per-operation cost is close to constant at roughly 600 microseconds regardless of tensor size: a fill on a 49-element tensor occupies the host for 664 microseconds while its kernel runs for about 1 microsecond. A cost that does not scale with the data is submission-path cost, not work. The dispatches originate in the Qwen3 causal-LM forward pass, and the call chains show the model already running under a compiled and ahead-of-time-traced wrapper, so graph-level compilation is in place but per-operation submission is not being elided. (source: `cpu_idle_metrics.json` → `gpu_utilization.idle_time_percent`, `gpu_utilization.idle_time_ms`; `category_manifest.json` → `categories[].sync_time_ms`, `categories[].has_sync_bottleneck`; `multi_kernel_data.json` → `overlap_analysis.exposed_comm_time_us`, `overlap_analysis.exposed_memcpy_time_us`)

**Data:**

| Metric | Value | Flagged |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Idle | 873.7 ms (50.9%) | true |
| Computation | 844.7 ms (49.1%) | false |
| Communication | 0.0 ms (0.0%) | false |
| MemCpy | 0.1 ms (0.0%) | false |
| Host duration in excess of kernel time | 691.5 ms (79.1% of idle) | true |
| Operations where host duration exceeds kernel time by more than 5x | 71 | true |
| Small-operation dispatches (elementwise, norm, Triton, other) | 1416 of 2144 (66.0%) | true |
| GPU kernel time from those dispatches | 93.0 ms (11.0%) | true |

**Flagged** marks metrics whose threshold is exceeded. Idle exceeds the 15% flag threshold. The host-excess and sync-operation rows are flagged because host duration exceeds kernel time by more than the 5x screening ratio. The small-operation rows are flagged because two thirds of all dispatches return only one ninth of the kernel time.

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** The GPU finishes the work it is given and then waits. Kernel time totals 844.7 ms against a 1718.4 ms window, so the device is fed for less than half the elapsed time. The host, by contrast, is occupied inside operation dispatch for 1536.2 ms, or about 89% of the same window. The host is therefore the pacing element, and the GPU idles behind it. The submission cost does not track tensor size, so it is not amortized by larger batches. It is paid once per operation. Two thirds of the dispatches in the window are small operations that return only 11.0% of the kernel time, so the majority of the submission cost buys very little device work. The problem compounds with depth rather than width: at 36 layers and roughly 536 dispatches per forward pass, each additional layer adds submission cost that the device cannot overlap.

**Resolution:** Graph capture changes what the host submits. Instead of walking the operation list and paying the submission cost 536 times per pass, the host enqueues one pre-recorded launch sequence, and the per-operation host path disappears from the critical path entirely. This addresses the constant-cost component directly, which is the component the data shows dominating. Capture requires fixed shapes, and the batches here vary from 1072 to 8192 tokens, so padding to shape buckets is the enabling step; the largest mixed prefill batches may remain uncapturable. For those, reducing the dispatch count is the alternative lever on the same quantity, because submission cost is per operation: collapsing the normalization, cache-write and activation chain into fewer launches removes submissions rather than making each one cheaper. Both routes shrink the same 691.5 ms term.

**Impact estimate:** Impact estimate is not quantifiable from trace data.

<a id="detailed-analysis-system-p2"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=system rank=2 -->
#### 🟡 P2: Host-side preparation inside the attention wrapper stalls the pipeline

**Identification:** The attention path was examined separately because it carries the largest host gap per invocation of any operation in the trace. Across 144 invocations the wrapper occupies the host for 297.9 ms while its kernels run for 121.4 ms, a gap of 176.5 ms, or 1.23 ms per call. The gap is not proportional to the kernel work behind it: one shape group runs 8.1 ms of kernels across 36 calls yet holds the host for 74.2 ms. The wrapper is entered once per decoder layer from the Qwen3 attention layer, so the cost repeats 36 times per forward pass. Its kernels are the paged-attention and forward-attention kernels on a single stream. (source: `category_manifest.json` → `categories[].cpu_duration_ms`, `categories[].gpu_kernel_time_ms`, `categories[].sync_time_ms` for `inferenceattention`; `inferenceattention_ops.csv` → `total_duration_us`, `Kernel Time (µs)_sum`, `operation_count`, `entry_point`, `call_stack_full`)

**Data:**

| Metric | Value | Flagged |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Attention host-side duration | 297.9 ms | true |
| Attention GPU kernel time | 121.4 ms | false |
| Host duration in excess of kernel time | 176.5 ms (20.2% of idle) | true |
| Invocations | 144 | false |
| Host gap per invocation | 1.23 ms | true |
| Lowest-kernel shape group: kernel time | 8.1 ms over 36 calls | false |
| Lowest-kernel shape group: host duration | 74.2 ms over 36 calls | true |

**Flagged** marks metrics whose threshold is exceeded. The host-excess rows are flagged because host duration exceeds kernel time by more than the 5x screening ratio applied to this category.

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** The host time inside this wrapper is 2.5 times its own kernel time, and it does not fall when the kernel work falls. A shape group whose kernels run for 8.1 ms still holds the host for 74.2 ms. Cost that stays flat as device work shrinks is fixed per-call host work, not a wait on the device. Because the wrapper sits on the per-layer critical path and is entered 36 times per pass, this fixed cost is multiplied by model depth. The wrapper duration may also enclose nested operations dispatched inside it, so part of the gap is nested dispatch cost rather than work unique to the wrapper; either way it is host work standing between consecutive attention kernel launches. During that interval the device has nothing queued from this path.

**Resolution:** Attention metadata such as block tables, sequence lengths and slot mappings is a property of the batch, not of the layer, so it does not change between the 36 per-layer calls within a pass. Computing it once per pass and passing it down removes 35 of every 36 evaluations from the critical path, converting the per-layer call into a kernel submission. This attacks redundancy in the call path, which is a different quantity from the per-dispatch submission cost in the first finding, so the two reductions are additive. Confirming which part of the 1.23 ms gap is the wrapper's own work versus nested dispatches requires a host-side profile of the attention call, which a kernel trace does not resolve.

**Impact estimate:** Impact estimate is not quantifiable from trace data.
